column1: # Agents set to run commands without asking. One line each, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   agent     as the report shows it
#   os        all, mac, linux or win (win is Git Bash and gird-check.ps1)
#   path      the settings file, with the path tokens data/sessions.tsv uses, or {PROJECT}/folder/file
#             for that file in every project folder the home scan finds. One folder may be *, for that
#             file in every folder there (VS Code keeps a settings file for each profile)
#   setting   as the report shows it
#   pattern   one or more, each in its own field, and every one must match. Spaces are ignored. A
#             .json file is read as one line (the scripts' flat): a match starts at the text, a { or
#             a , and ends at the text's end, a , } # or /, so a longer key or another value never
#             counts. A pattern written "key": {... matches its rest that way, and only directly
#             inside the object that top-level key holds. A .toml file is read line by line: a line
#             starting with # is skipped, a match is a whole line (up to a # comment), so a setting
#             inside an inline table does not count, a value in double quotes also matches the same
#             value in single quotes (a TOML literal string), and only the lines before the first
#             [table] count (a setting under [profiles.x] applies only when that profile is used, and
#             Codex 0.134.0 and later read no such table from config.toml). A pattern !key, in a .toml
#             file only and beside another pattern, matches when none of those lines sets that key
# Claude Code: code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes, and its settings reference, where defaultMode
# is a key of permissions and of nothing else. Codex: its configuration reference, and its
# advanced configuration page for profiles (0.134.0). Its permissions page (beta): the built-in
# profile :danger-full-access, chosen with default_permissions, removes the sandbox, and replaces the
# older sandbox_mode. For a file that sets both, Codex's docs and code disagree: the permissions page
# says sandbox_mode then wins and not to set both, while the code (0.164.0, resolve_permission_config_syntax)
# uses the profile when one file sets both. The lines follow the code: the sandbox_mode line counts only
# in a file that sets no default_permissions.
# TOML's literal strings: toml.io. VS Code:
# the Copilot settings reference and the 1.104 release notes. VS Code 1.104 renamed chat.tools.autoApprove
# to chat.tools.global.autoApprove without migrating it, so the old name is ignored, and it reads the
# new one from the user settings only (scope APPLICATION_MACHINE in its source), never from a
# project's .vscode/settings.json. A project's chat.tools.autoApprove is the setting CVE-2025-53773
# wrote; section 2 of the scripts lists it as a sign of that attack, not as a setting in force.
# VS Code added chat.permissions.default, the permission level new chats start with: autoApprove
# ("Allow all" in the chat's permission picker and "Bypass Approvals" in the Settings editor, at VS Code
# 1.143.1) and autopilot run every tool call without asking (VS Code's AI settings reference and
# approvals page; the values and labels from chat.shared.contribution.ts and
# permissionPickerActionItem.ts). It declares no scope, and VS Code reads its merged value, so a
# project's .vscode/settings.json sets it too: section 2 of the scripts lists such a project's copy,
# as a setting a cloned project brings, not as a line here.
# chat.defaultConfiguration, an object whose approvals and mode would have to be read inside it, is
# not read.
# Claude Code's VS Code extension: its docs (the VS Code and permission-modes pages) say that
# claudeCode.initialPermissionMode set to bypassPermissions in the user settings starts new conversations
# in bypass mode only with claudeCode.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions on (without it they start in
# Manual), and that it reads the first from the user settings only, so both must match there. The
# extension installs in Cursor too, where the docs give it an install link; Cursor keeps its user
# settings in Cursor/User as VS Code does in Code/User. A settings file that holds two agents' settings
# makes a row for each.
# VS Code profiles: VS Code's settings docs put a profile's user settings in
# Code/User/profiles/<profile ID>/settings.json, in force while that profile is active. VS Code's source
# (PROFILE_SCOPES in workbench/services/configuration) reads machine, window and resource settings from
# a profile's file, never application ones. chat.permissions.default declares no scope (window), and
# the Claude Code extension declares both its settings machine (its package.json, 2.1.310): each has a
# profile line. chat.tools.global.autoApprove is APPLICATION_MACHINE, read from the default profile only,
# so it has none. VS Code Insiders keeps its user data in a folder named after its product's nameShort
# (src/mainImpl.ts), Code - Insiders in the Insiders build's product.json, with the same settings.
# Cursor has VS Code's profiles (its docs on importing a VS Code profile), kept the same way.
